implementation_notes: Rust statics must be constant-initialized, so there is no dynamic static initialization order to fiasco; first-use construction is provided by std::sync, not by language syntax. OnceLock<T> (stable 1.70) holds a value written once via get_or_init and can live in a static; LazyLock<T, F> (stable 1.80) adds the deref-to-value convenience for the common case where the initializer is fixed at the declaration, and std::sync::Once remains for one-time side effects without a value. Choose LazyLock for a plain lazy static, OnceLock when the value must be set conditionally or later, and remember the classic guard object is simply not needed here.
pitfalls: OnceLock::get_or_init leaves the cell uninitialized if the initializer panics (later callers retry), while LazyLock poisons irrecoverably - after a panicking initializer every later access panics - and Once::call_once poisons too; wrap fallible setup in a Result instead of panicking.
Recursive initialization is unspecified: calling get_or_init inside the initializer of the same cell currently deadlocks, and Rust's borrow checker cannot catch that case.
Statics are never dropped: no destructor runs at program exit, so flush/close/unregister work needs an explicit shutdown path rather than Drop.
Do not reach for `static mut`: the cell types exist so that one-time initialization is expressed without unsafe aliasing.

variants.name: std::sync::LazyLock (stable since Rust 1.80)
variants.idiom_name: static LazyLock::new(...) with deref on first access
variants.implementation_notes: LazyLock wraps the initialization closure and derefs to &T, so the accessor function disappears: the first dereference initializes, later ones are plain reads, and concurrent readers block until the initializer finishes. Prefer it when the initializer is known at the declaration site; keep OnceLock when the value must be supplied later or conditionally.
pitfalls: Poisoning is irrecoverable: a panicking initializer makes every later access panic (unlike OnceLock::get_or_init, which leaves the cell uninitialized).
Declaring the holder as const instead of static compiles but creates a fresh value on every use; the crate documentation calls out this trap explicitly.

variants.name: once_cell::sync::{OnceCell, Lazy} (pre-std toolchains)
variants.implementation_notes: Before the standard library stabilized OnceLock and LazyLock, once_cell supplied the same idea: sync::OnceCell for explicit get_or_init and sync::Lazy for a lazy static, both thread-safe and usable from statics. It remains the portable choice for older MSRVs or no_std targets, and its documentation shows the standard global-data recipes (logger, global map, lazily compiled regex).
pitfalls: The holder must be a static, not a const: the docs warn that the const version compiles but re-creates the value on every use.
Optional features (for example parking_lot) raise the effective minimum compiler version beyond what the plain crate requires.
